title: Formex Essence Ceramica Dark Matter Redshift pairs full ceramic with a meteorite dial
excerpt: Full black ceramic case, bracelet and clasp, a solid Muonionalusta meteorite dial with red accents, and a COSC Sellita SW200-2 Power+ inside. Formex builds 100 a year at $4,450.
content:

Full ceramic usually means a big-house price. Ceramic cases show up on flagship sports watches, and ceramic bracelets push the bill even higher.

Formex took a different route. Its new Formex Essence Ceramica Dark Matter Redshift pairs a full black ceramic case and bracelet with a solid meteorite dial, and it lands at $4,450.

Price: $4,450
Where to buy: Formex

Ceramic from case to clasp

Zirconium oxide ceramic covers nearly everything you touch. Case, bezel, bracelet and clasp all use it.

Formex finishes most surfaces with a sandblasted matte texture. Diamond-polished bevels cut along the edges, so light catches the case lines instead of the whole watch glowing.

Specs stay wearable. Diameter is 41mm, height is 11.2mm, and lug-to-lug is 46.2mm.

Case weight is just 56 grams before the bracelet. Ceramic is hard, light and hypoallergenic, and Formex says it is virtually scratchproof in daily use.

Four springs sit between the upper and lower case. Formex calls it the Case Suspension System, and it is built to absorb shocks while letting the case move a little on the wrist.

Water resistance is 100 meters. Sapphire covers the front and the back, with anti-reflective treatment on the inside.

Ceramic punishes sloppy machining. Hardness that resists scratches also resists cutting and finishing, and Formex brings 40 years of ceramic component manufacturing to this case and bracelet.

That background shows in the edges. Bevels stay sharp, links line up clean, and polished accents land exactly where the sandblasted surfaces end.

A dial cut from space rock

Solid Muonionalusta meteorite forms the dial. Formex cuts a slice, etches it, and finishes it with a black-gold galvanic coating under one micron thick.

Etching reveals the Widmanstätten pattern. Iron and nickel cooled over millions of years in space, and the interlocking crystals left a structure no two dials share.

Color runs deep anthracite to near black. Texture does the work here, shifting as light moves across the surface.

Red breaks the blackout. A red seconds hand, red lettering and red chapter-ring marks give the dial its Redshift name, drawn from light stretching toward red as objects recede.

Dial feet are soldered straight to the meteorite. Iron content makes that possible, so Formex skips the brass base most meteorite dials need and runs a thicker solid dial instead.

A beveled date window sits at 6 o’clock. Applied gunmetal indices carry BGW9 Super-LumiNova, and the hour and minute hands match in gunmetal with brushed faces and polished bevels.

Muonionalusta is among the oldest known materials on Earth. Formex leans into that contrast, ancient space rock inside a case built with modern ceramic tooling.

Name aside, execution stays restrained. Red appears in small doses, and the meteorite pattern carries the dial instead of a printed design sitting on top of it.

COSC power with a longer reserve

Sellita’s SW200-2 Power+ sits inside a Grade 2 titanium container. Each movement is tested and certified by COSC, Switzerland’s official chronometer institute.

Certification means an average daily rate between -4 and +6 seconds across positions and temperatures. That is chronometer grade, not a marketing label.

Power reserve is 65 hours. You can set it down on Friday and pick it up on Monday still running.

Details show through the sapphire back. A custom skeleton rotor turns over thermally blued screws, with 26 jewels and a glucydur balance wheel inside.

A ceramic clasp that adjusts on the wrist

Ceramic bracelets usually force a compromise. You size it once with pins, and you live with that fit when your wrist swells or shrinks.

Formex built micro-adjustment into the ceramic clasp itself. Formex calls it the first on-the-fly system of its kind in a full ceramic bracelet.

Adjustment covers 5mm in four steps of 1.25mm. You change it in seconds, with no tools and without taking the watch off.

Links taper from 22mm to 20mm. Pin and tube links handle sizing, a tool is included, and the quick-release system lets straps swap by hand in seconds.

Rubber, nylon and Italian leather straps are sold as add-ons. Each runs on Formex’s carbon fiber composite deployant clasp, with its own 7mm gradual micro-adjustment you can work on the wrist.

Small run, direct route

Production stays tight. Formex builds 100 pieces a year, and the first series is numbered 001 to 100.

Pre-orders run first come, first served. First shipments are scheduled for the end of November, in the order orders arrived.

Price is $4,450 on the ceramic bracelet. For US delivery, that figure includes tariffs and duties, with local sales tax calculated at checkout and shipping included worldwide on Formex orders.

Put the spec list beside flagship ceramic sports watches and the gap is clear. You get full ceramic, a solid meteorite dial and a certified chronometer movement, without paying flagship money for ceramic alone.

Buyers who want ceramic without the flagship tax are the audience here. Collectors chasing a meteorite dial that is solid, dark and actually different from the next one should look closely too.

Formex is an independent, family-owned maker based in Biel/Bienne. Every watch is designed, developed and assembled in-house there, and coverage runs to a three-year international warranty.

Price: $4,450
Where to buy: Formex

Orders are open now through Formex, with that first numbered batch shipping at the end of November.
